clue.text: Brussels offers a prize for good nutrition …

parts.note: Brussels is the seat of the European Union, so it stands for EU
a trophy is a prize such as a cup or shield

explanation.surface: The European capital hands out an award for healthy eating, with the sentence running on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this clue to 5 across, but each clue is complete on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: The rare word is a technical term for a healthy state of nourishment in a body or organism.

clue.text: In the event it will disappear

definitions.text: In the event it will disappear

parts.words: In the event it will disappear
parts.note: a state of looking forward to something ends once the thing actually happens

explanation.surface: A remark that something will vanish when the occasion comes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the event' looks like a mere phrase meaning 'as it turned out', but it is literal: once the awaited event arrives, waiting for it is over.
explanation.definitionFit: Anticipation of something ceases once that thing actually takes place.

clue.text: Monstrous production of Tony with great Euro disaster

indicators.note: a disaster leaves things in ruins, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
E is the symbol abbreviation for the euro

explanation.surface: Tony Blair's grand European plan turns into a monstrous fiasco.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disaster' rearranges TONY, GREAT and E (euro) together.
explanation.definitionFit: The rare scientific term means the producing of monsters, that is malformed offspring.

clue.text: Old Egyptian believer loses head and eye

indicators.note: its first letter is cut off

parts.note: the Coptic church is the ancient Christian church of Egypt

explanation.surface: An ancient Egyptian Christian is beheaded and loses an eye.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a jocular or technical noun for the eye, as well as the adjective about sight.

clue.text: Connoisseur of tapestry, like the Lord of Wem?

definitions.meaning: someone who assesses wall hangings, read literally
Judge Jeffreys, Baron Jeffreys of Wem, was notorious for sending people to the gallows after the 1685 Monmouth Rebellion

explanation.surface: An art expert compared with a notorious seventeenth-century peer.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase normally means a judge who readily passes death sentences; the first reading treats it as someone who judges hangings, that is tapestries.
explanation.definitionFit: Hangings are tapestries, so a judge of them is a connoisseur; and Jeffreys of the Bloody Assizes was the classic harsh sentencer.

clue.text: … favouring growth, which could be one 15

definitions.meaning: ... in an older sense means warm and kindly to life, encouraging things to grow
in anatomy ... means relating to the chin, so a measurement at the chin could be described this way, tying to 15 across

explanation.surface: Continuing 1 across: good nutrition encourages growth, which might be measured at some slant.
explanation.walkthrough: The usual meaning, friendly, is not used: one sense is 'favourable to growth', the other is the anatomical sense from the Greek for chin.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dictionary senses: a mild climate encouraging plants, and an anatomical adjective about the chin.

clue.text: Offspring with the greatest 1 down

parts.note: the 1 down answer, prospects or anticipation, is greatest for the child first in line to inherit

explanation.surface: The child with the greatest prospects.
explanation.walkthrough: Under primogeniture the firstborn male inherits, so he has the greatest expectations.
explanation.definitionFit: The firstborn male child traditionally inherits title and estate, so he has most to look forward to.

clue.text: Island on one island

parts.note: taken as written
a means one, the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An island lying on top of another island.
explanation.walkthrough: The first word, not the last, is wordplay; the final 'island' is the definition, the Hebridean isle where St Columba founded his monastery.
explanation.definitionFit: This small isle in the Inner Hebrides of Scotland is famous for its abbey.

clue.text: Tepid evangelist?

parts.note: an evangelist whose name begins the word for tepid, as if he preached half-heartedly

explanation.surface: A preacher who is only lukewarm about his message.
explanation.walkthrough: Lukewarm means tepid; take off 'warm' and the remainder names one of the four Gospel writers.
explanation.definitionFit: This writer of the third Gospel is one of the four evangelists, and his name starts the word for tepid.

clue.text: Hardly the occupation of Holy Jack?

definitions.text: Hardly the occupation of Holy Jack?

parts.words: Hardly the occupation of Holy Jack?
parts.note: split the word as PI (pious, holy) plus RATING (a jack, an ordinary sailor): a pious sailor would hardly take to robbery at sea

explanation.surface: A pious sailor is the last person you would expect to take up a life of crime on the high seas.
explanation.walkthrough: PI is crossword shorthand for pious and a rating or jack is an ordinary seaman, so the answer splits into a holy jack, whose job it hardly is.
explanation.definitionFit: Robbing ships at sea is the trade of a buccaneer, which a devout seaman would hardly practise.

clue.text: French hop curtailed in Greek port

indicators.note: the shortened French dance sits inside the abbreviation
cut short at its tail, so the final letter of the French word goes

parts.note: danse is the French word for a dance, and a hop is an informal dance

explanation.surface: A French dance cut short in a harbour town of Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek port' looks like a single definition, but Greek is wordplay (GK) and only 'port' defines: the city is on the Polish Baltic coast.
explanation.definitionFit: This city is Poland's chief seaport on the Baltic, formerly called Danzig.

clue.text: Scheme for PLA

parts.note: the clue's three letters are the word for a scheme with its tail cut off, so a de-tailed version of it

explanation.surface: A plan for the Chinese army, the PLA.
explanation.walkthrough: Detailed is read as de-tailed, losing its last letter: the four-letter word for a scheme minus its tail is PLA.
explanation.definitionFit: A thorough scheme worked out item by item is a full blueprint for action.

clue.text: Sort of teachers (sic)

indicators.note: to sort letters is to rearrange them, so the following words are reshuffled

explanation.surface: A note that a particular kind of teacher is meant, with a (sic) to show the odd wording is deliberate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' rearranges TEACHERS plus SIC; the whole clue also describes the answer, people who teach by question and answer.
explanation.definitionFit: These are religious instructors who teach doctrine through a fixed series of questions and answers.

clue.text: In pain but passed on without hardship

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the word for died goes around the other

parts.note: to pass on is a euphemism for to die
stress is strain or hardship

explanation.surface: Someone suffering, though they died without hardship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' here means outside, not lacking.
explanation.definitionFit: To be suffering anguish or pain is to be in this state.

clue.text: Blair's in tears — oddly, having a hard look

indicators.note: the possessive name goes inside the rearranged letters
done oddly, the letters of the word are arranged in an unusual way

parts.note: Tony Blair, former British prime minister, gives his first name with the possessive

explanation.surface: Tony Blair is crying, but strangely he is giving someone a hard look.
explanation.walkthrough: Blair's first name is Tony, so 'Blair's' gives the name plus S. 'oddly' turns TEARS into STARE, and the name goes inside that, after its S. 'Oddly' looks like it means take the odd letters, but here it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixed, cold, unblinking gaze is a hard look.

clue.text: Bernician fish

definitions.meaning: Bernicia was an early medieval kingdom in northern England founded by the Germanic people who gave England its name
to fish with a rod and line

explanation.surface: Someone from an old northern English kingdom described as a kind of fish.
explanation.walkthrough: Bernicia was an Anglo-Saxon kingdom covering what is now Northumberland and south-east Scotland, settled by one of those Germanic tribes.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a member of that Germanic tribe; the other is the verb for fishing with hook and line.

clue.text: A nice pure treat for the fastidious

indicators.note: to treat something is to process it, so the letters are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: A lovely pure delicacy for the fussy eater.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treat' looks like a noun, a delicacy, but acts as a verb rearranging A NICE PURE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone devoted to refined pleasures, especially food, is fastidious in their tastes.

clue.text: Change of clothing in the car?

definitions.text: Change of clothing in the car?

parts.words: Change of clothing in the car?
parts.note: read gear as clothing and shift as change, but in a car the phrase is the lever or act of moving between gears

explanation.surface: Someone getting changed in the back seat of a car.
explanation.walkthrough: Gear is slang for clothes, so the surface suggests changing outfits in a vehicle; motoring sense is the selection of a different gear.
explanation.definitionFit: In a car, moving from one gear ratio to another is this action, also the American word for the gear lever.

clue.text: Actor in film, Greek character with a line constantly repeated

parts.note: Tom Conti is a Scottish stage and film actor
nu is the thirteenth letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A film actor and a Greek figure share a line that keeps being repeated.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Conti, the Scottish actor of Shirley Valentine, supplies the first five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that keeps happening again and again is described with this adjective, as in endless interruptions.

clue.text: 12's about time to get off, which is impracticable

indicators.note: the midday word goes around the abbreviation for time

parts.note: twelve o'clock in the day is midday, so the number stands for that time

explanation.surface: The religious teacher of 12 across says it is high time to dismount, which cannot be done.
explanation.walkthrough: '12' looks like a cross-reference to 12 across but is just the number, read as midday. The phrase meaning off or cancelled is also an idiom for something unacceptable or impracticable.
explanation.definitionFit: The two-word phrase means cancelled or off, and also describes a plan that cannot be carried out.

clue.text: Not the way of a believer, unless doing wrong

definitions.text: Not the way of a believer

indicators.note: the word doing is itself fodder, and wrong says those letters are put out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A believer would not behave like this unless he were doing wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doing' does double duty in the surface only: in the parse it is fodder, and 'wrong' alone signals the rearrangement of UNLESS DOING.
explanation.definitionFit: Irreligious or wicked conduct is the opposite of how a devout person behaves.

clue.text: Plant in no uncertain terms

indicators.note: the answer is found inside the run of letters

explanation.surface: Planting something with a very forceful explanation.
explanation.walkthrough: The familiar phrase 'in no uncertain terms' disguises the device; Plant means bury.
explanation.definitionFit: To plant in the ground in the sense of burying a body is to lay it in a grave.

clue.text: Bath, say, many download from the net

parts.note: Bath is an English city famous as a spa town
M, the Roman numeral for a thousand, stands for many

explanation.surface: Lots of people in Bath download things from the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: Bath is a Somerset city known for its Roman baths, so it is an example of a spa.
explanation.definitionFit: Junk email arrives unwanted from the internet, so it is something downloaded from the net.

clue.text: It's wrong to put up with a left-winger

indicators.note: in a down entry, put up means the word is written bottom to top

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law

explanation.surface: Tolerating a socialist is a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up with' reads as tolerate, but 'put up' is the reversal and 'with a' just links. The answer is short for Trotskyist.
explanation.definitionFit: A Trotskyist is a far-left socialist, so the short form names a left-winger.

clue.text: Lady of ill report

indicators.note: something ill is out of sorts, so the letters of the next word are set badly

explanation.surface: A woman with a bad reputation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lady of ill repute' is the expected phrase; the Lady is Dame Shirley Porter, Tesco heiress and Westminster council leader censured over the homes-for-votes scandal.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Shirley Porter, wife of Sir Leslie Porter, was widely known as Lady Porter.

clue.text: One's got it in the neck for taking time in drama degree

definitions.text: One's got it in the neck

indicators.note: the word for drama takes in the abbreviation for time

parts.note: drama as a body of work means plays
an MA is a Master of Arts degree

explanation.surface: Someone getting a scolding while studying for a theatre qualification.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got it in the neck' sounds like being punished, but here it is literal: the answer is a muscle located in the neck.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a broad thin sheet of muscle running down each side of the neck from jaw to collarbone.

clue.text: Rising by the minute, a women's organisation

parts.note: MU is the Mothers' Union, a Christian women's organisation
minute in the sense of very small means tiny

explanation.surface: A women's group grows by the minute.
explanation.walkthrough: The Mothers' Union is an Anglican charity for women.
explanation.definitionFit: A rising is an uprising or revolt, and a revolt of sailors or soldiers is this.

clue.text: Loosen mixed bundle containing work of 12

indicators.note: the jumbled letters hold the next piece inside
a mixed collection is jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: RI is religious instruction, the job of the teachers at 12 across

explanation.surface: Untie a mixed parcel that contains some religious teaching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed' turns BUNDLE into UNBDLE. The cross-reference to 12 across, the religious teachers, points to the abbreviation for religious instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To remove a horse's bridle is to free it, so the verb means to set loose or release.
